subtopic: GEORGE D. BROWN FARM, PAKENHAM, ONT.
GEORGE D. BROWN FARM, PAKENHAM, ONT.
speechtext:
1.	Is the Pakenham farm operated by George D. Brown a test farm as laid down in the January 14, 1965, news release?
2.	If the answer to the above is yes, will the government produce account books for the two years the farm has been in operation so that the economics of the model can be examined?
3.	If the answer to the first question is no, how many test farms have been set up as suggested in the January 14, 1965, news release and where are they?
4.	Does the government own the farm on which this experiment is being carried out at Pakenham and, if so, does it consider it typical marginal farm land?
5.	To the knowledge of the government, does George D. Brown have hired help on his farm and, if so, who pays them and how much?
6.	Are there any other cattle on the farm other than those owned by the federal government?
7.	In the experiments carried out with grade Holstein cows, what beef breeds are being used, how many cows to each breed, and why are grade Holstein cows being used?
8.	Are the cows milked and do they nurse the calf at the same time and, if so, is a thorough accounting done to realize the net gain?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: GEORGE D. BROWN FARM, PAKENHAM, ONT.
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	The farm test has been in operation less than two years of the three year experimental period. Reports of the economics of operation are planned for publication following the conclusion of the experiment.
3.	N/A.
4.	No, the farm is owned by Mr. Brown.
5.	George D. Brown has hired help on his. farm but this help is paid for by Mr. Brown and the rate of pay is not known to this department.
6.	There are no other milk cows on this farm. Mr. Brown does, however, buy feeder cattle periodically and finish them for market, strictly as his own project.
7.	The beef breeds used are Charolais and Hereford. The former is used for artificial breeding purposes and the latter for breeding those cows which have not conceived artificially.
The basis of the experiment was a Holstein-Charolais cross for use by dairy farmers having grade Holstein cows.
Grade Holstein cows are the bases of the majority of dairy herds and the Holstein-Charolais cross was used to produce big meaty calves as rapidly as possible.
8.	The calves are separated from the cows in the evening and the cows are pastured during the night with a milkout in the morning. The calves are then turned back with, the cows.
A detailed accounting is being done with, respect to the economics of operation.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Batten in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word or two on this subject, in summary of my remarks made last evening. I was trying to point out at that time that the unification of our armed forces was a drastic change in the whole defence picture and would have effects on the very sovereignty of which Canadians have been so proud over the years. I was asking the minister to allow us the same privilege of which the associate minister availed himself and which he exercised in his speech to the house. The associate minister said that he also wondered whether or not this was the right policy. He paused, he hesitated, he consulted experts and they reassured him that this was the right policy. All we on this side are asking of the minister is the same right as was exercised by the Associate Minister of National Defence. We want to call in witnesses who we think are capable of giving us a clear picture of the situation. I do not know what witnesses the minister or the associate minister called in, but we see today all across Canada numerous former officers from the navy, the army and the air force coming forward and expressing grave doubts as to the whole idea of unification.
Editorials in every leading paper are questioning the procedure suggested by the minister. I could read editorials from the Calgary Herald, the Vancouver newspapers, the Globe and Mail and even the Winnipeg Free Press questioning whether or not this house should

pause to consider and hear evidence before voting on the principle of the bill.
Last evening the minister stated that all he wanted to do was to follow the normal course. I suggest to him that the normal course is the proper one to follow in a normal case, but at this time the house is being asked to break away from normal and traditional procedure. The house has previously departed from normal procedure in dealing with legislation. I remember quite well when Bill No. C-120, the new transportation bill, was introduced a couple of years ago. The Minister of Transport realized that it represented a drastic change in the whole transportation system in Canada and he asked for unanimous consent to delay second reading of the bill so as to send it to a committee for further detailed examination. He received the unanimous consent of the house and the bill did go to committee. It proved to be unworkable and was thrown out.
It seems to me this was a factual appraisal of a piece of government legislation. One might say it was democracy at work. This is all we ask of the Minister of National Defence. We beg him and we plead with him to let us examine this bill in committee. We have gone along with integration. I have nothing against integration of the personnel in the armed forces. However, we want to pause now and see whether this integration should develop into the ultimate unification or amalgamation of the services.
The Minister of National Defence or the Prime Minister might well say that the opposition is terrible because it is using blackmail, that by prolonging debate on this supply motion we are placing the government in a dangerous financial crisis. We have nothing like that in mind. It is the government alone which has placed itself in this position.
Two or three weeks ago the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona asked that his motion be sent to a committee. He had to have the unanimous consent of the house, and it received the support of every member in this house, except the minister, who said "I alone refuse". That is where he made a grave mistake, and I emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that he was the only one to refuse unanimous consent.
There were many members on the other side of the house who agreed. In fact I think I heard even the Prime Minister say he agreed. The only one to say "no" was the Minister of National Defence.
November 9, 1966
He is in control of the Liberal caucus.

He may well be. We are pleading with the minister to solve his own financial crisis and not to blame us for having created it. He alone created it some two or three weeks ago when he was the only one to rise in his place and refuse unanimous consent.
I say to the minister that he is not asking the house to take the normal course with regard to unification, that in reality it represents a drastic change. In those circumstances I think it is only wise to follow the example set by that venerable politician, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, when he suggested that before second reading the railway bill be submitted to a committee. Maybe the Minister of National Defence being a younger member in the house, does not have the political experience of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, but he should follow his example.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
For example let us look at some of the evidence as it appeared in today's Citizen in which appears an article written by Vice Admiral Rayner, who is just one of a whole host of 40 officers who retired earlier at a cost of nearly $1 million to the taxpayers. Vice Admiral Rayner had been a naval officer for 30 years but he retired of his own accord. This is what he has said about one of the matters mentioned last night, our sovereignty:
I think that the sovereignty of our nation is bound up with the question of unification.
This is a statement that cannot be dismissed lightly because this naval officer has had 30 years' experience serving his country. I am reading this article to help all those on whom the burden rests of deciding whether or not we should unify our forces, and this includes every citizen of Canada.
Then the Vice Admiral goes on to quote the following statement, and I think this is particularly directed to members of the House of Commons.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Vice Admiral Rayner continues by quoting these words, to which I believe he is directing the attention of hon. members;
I say it would be absolutely unforgiveable and indefensible if this house were asked to commit itself to this very important principle of unification, which the minister himself has described as a fundamental reorganization, before the views of qualified and experienced persons have been expressed.
I would ask all members of the house to consider that statement. The minister alone can resolve the position in which the government finds itself today. He alone can assure all civil servants across Canada that they will receive their pay on time. The burden of responsibility rests on him. Therefore I urge him to stand in his place and say that he is tired of the supply debate going on and on. Let him say that he has nothing to conceal, that he wants to reveal the facts and to send this matter to the defence committee. That is all we ask.
I will not hold it against him if he does this. If somebody says that he has retreated, I would say that he has become wise and has become wise not too late. This will save the nation an embarrassment, it will save the government from mishandling the affairs of the country, and it will bring about some degree of satisfaction to the admirals, generals and air vice marshals who are concerned about our defences and about the sovereignty upon which Canada depends so much.

Mr. Chairman, in all modesty, I admit that I did not feel any special competence to comment in this house on the matter of national defence. However, I think that during these few last days it has become clear that the debate is taking a very specific course which goes beyond the field of national defence and, as a matter of fact, the debate is now rather on the question of national security. As a Canadian and as a member of parliament, I believe that I am bound to make some comments, more particularly because of two incidents that occurred last week end, which have shown me that there is more at stake than the matter raised up to now by the Minister of National Defence.

November 9, 1966
Interim Supply
The first was a rather dull speech given last Friday, I believe, by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain). I had intended to make a few teasing remarks to say the least, about him, but unfortunately I hear that he is not only away from the house but out of the country; I shall therefore contain myself in that respect. Still, I should like to point out that it is rather strange that that independent member should always find a way of supporting, and most staunchly, the positions adopted by the government. In every debate he always goes to the rescue of the poor little Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), of the poor little Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith). Running true to form, last Friday he went to the rescue of the poor little Minister of National Defence.
I feel that if he is to follow so steadfastly the Liberal stand he should not be ashamed -because one must not be ashamed-to be a Liberal, all the more so because, at the present time, it seems that the members of that party could use all the support they can get no matter where it comes from.
But the point I wanted to make with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, is that he claims he is willing to accept blindly and straight away the principle which is being defended here. That astonishes me for the particular reason that ever since that question has come up, more and more doubts have been expressed from day to day, from week to week and from month to month. There is also decreasing recruitment in the armed forces and an increasing number of resignations. Everything revolves on the debate on that principle.
Now, it has been established that the armed forces need approximately 109,000 men; we are getting closer to that figure all the time. To be logical, we must anticipate the day when the armed forces will comprise less than 109,000 men-perhaps 90,000 or 85,000-always because of a questionable principle. Now, the normal consequence, if 109,000 men are really needed in our armed forces, is that the vacancies will have to be filled and the only way will be through conscription. I can hardly believe that the member for Trois-Rivieres, as well as the member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), would be ready to endorse without question a principle likely to bring about such a result.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, 1 think it is more and more obvious that members of the government are particularly good at living in a world of fiction, a world of make-believe. They have imputed all kinds of motives to us until now and I think little by little the message will get across that we are not here to enjoy ourselves, that they are raising a serious matter, a matter of principle which we will have to face. But we must not forget that it is also a matter for which they may have to answer one day, because they are taking a stand which is extremely difficult to defend and maintain; they may have to answer for it and we are surely taking down everything.
The second incident has to do with the fact that over the weekend I had the opportunity to meet a rather large number of air force officers and their wives. If the minister is under the impression that the whole matter is not creating doubts and weakening morale in our armed forces, I think he should make it his duty to go and see them. If he does not believe the officers he might listen more closely to their wives who are completely dismayed and are objecting more and more strongly to the measures which are to be imposed upon them, because they see that the opposition to the simple question which is raised give to understand that things are going on behind the scenes which can only play against them.
Strangely enough, in that group of 20 people or so, the only one who stood up for the minister's defence policy was a civil servant working for the air force. He had learned his lesson very well, obviously from that information source from which the minister gets the conviction he needs to defend his
stand.	.
Mr. Chairman, oddly enough that reminds me of the story of the fighter who was being clobbered round after round by a much better opponent. At the end of the first round, his trainer or second told him: "Do not worry, old man, he is not hitting you; your footwork is perfect, your defence is excellent." And so on until the eighth round. Always hearing the same thing, he asked his second: "Is it really true that he is not hitting me?" And the other one answered: "Yes." So the fighter said: "Well, watch the referee then
November 9, 1966

because someone is beating me up." I think that the minister would be well advised to listen a little less to his assistants and a little more to the people directly affected by the policy he wants to introduce.
Now, what is the question today? I think that at last the rather emotional tone of the first few hours of the debate has been dropped. I think quite frankly that the Canadian people, like everyone here, realize more and more that the question goes much deeper than Admiral Landymore, Admiral Brock or any other man.
The first question is unification. In spite of what the minister says, the meaning of that word is not understood at all, nor its effects.
He repeated several times last evening that it was simply a matter of following the normal trend of events.
I feel it must be realized that there is nothing normal in the present circumstances, because it is the first time in history, I believe, certainly in Canadian history and probably in American history, that such an attempt has been undertaken.
Then, since there is no precedent, I think it is entirely logical, before voting on the issue, to scrutinize as much as possible an entirely new principle and the minister is somewhat dishonest-Mr. Chairman, I apologize for using such an unparliamentary word, but I think you know in what state of mind it is used-to try to include, if you prefer, in a normal procedure, one which will create precedents which unfortunately are unknown to us.
It is in that sense that I maintain it is unfortunate to want us to accept a principle whose conclusions are unknown. And there again, the only thing the opposition asks is to be in a position to consider the question thoroughly before approving its principle.
They do not say it will be rejected. Above all, they definitely do not say "kill the bill". They only want to satisfy the normal curiosity of all Canadians and of all members of parliament who would like to know exactly what it is all about. This is therefore a unique fact.
But on the other hand, the stand we are taking is supported by precedents showing that the normal course is not necessarily always followed. Reference was made this afternoon to something which can be found on page 1057 of the Journals, and I quote:
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)

So we are not dealing with something new. We ask for special treatment in view of special conditions and circumstances before bringing in a unique form of national defence because we do not know enough about the matter.

For all that, enough doubts were created, because of the parties which stood up on both sides, to justify at least an intelligent question on the cogency of the principle intended to be laid down. I do not think that the Canadian people will blame us for taking a position based on logic.
In the second place, I am under the impression that this is more and more a question of an omniscient, omnipotent minister who wants to push through his point of view at all costs, even at the cost of our system of parliamentary committees from which, in principle, members derived much satisfaction.
Why is he jeopardizing the parliamentary committee system? This was mentioned before, and I will repeat it briefly. It is on account of the deplorable way, justified or not-I doubt very much that it can be justified-in which pieces of evidence by experts were handled, which has become obvious. Of course, if there is the least chance that civil service experts appearing before a parliamentary committee will receive suggestions or orders to be followed in one way, or another, we must certainly lose our faith in any communication we might get from the civil service.
I believe that this is a serious disadvantage and, in short, a legitimate concern. More and more this strength, this determination, this stubbornness on the part of the minister are becoming apparent and, it must be noted, he has received very little support, up to now, even from the people on his side.
There is another important point. We have been accused by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), by some members, and

I shall come back later on to the question of the civil service.
However, from a parliamentary point of view, we are entitled to a debate of 30 days on interim supply. So, the time that is needed to discuss this question, because it is worth discussing, is taken out of the time which we would normally devote to the study of other subjects during future debates.

However, in spite of all their efforts to whip it up into a "national issue", to dramatize the problem and create an atmosphere of deep concern, they have not been successful at all.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few grievances to air in the house, but on an entirely different subject from the ones stated by the previous speaker.
I should now like to call the attention of the house to a very important matter for the farmers and fruit-growers of my area.
In early June, two storms struck the area that I have the honour of representing in the house and caused extensive damage, to such an extent that according to a communication I received from the Societe Pomologique et fruitiere de Quebec, 170 farmers of my area have suffered damage estimated at approximately $2 million. Now, when I learned about this, I immediately got in touch with the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) to see whether he would contribute if the provincial government decided to give a subsidy to the stricken fanners; I was both disappointed and surprised by the attitude of the Minister of Agriculture since the members for the province of Quebec especially like to make us believe that he is the Minister of Agriculture who is most interested in the welfare and promotion of farmers in eastern Canada.
Hear, hear.

I hear the members opposite cheering. When I have finished speaking, I will ask those members if they are still of the same opinion and if they would wake up to join me and plead the cause of our farmers who are abandoned and ignored by the present Liberal government.
Mr. Chairman, I was saying that I have been disappointed by the position taken by the government and more particularly by the Minister of Agriculture. We got a flat refusal. The provincial minister of agriculture made representations upon his federal counterpart

to obtain assistance, but he also met with a refusal, which is a clear example of the way the federal minister wants to assist farmers in the province of Quebec. We therefore met with a flat no.
Now, the same refusal was met by southwestern Ontario farmers who, in the summer of 1964, lost all or almost all of their corn and tomato crops. Excessive rain early in the season followed by a severe drought destroyed completely the crops of the farmers in that area. They also got in touch with the federal Minister of Agriculture and were turned down flat. They were given the same answer as that given by the minister to the farmers of the province of Quebec. It went more or less like this: a crop insurance scheme has been approved by the House of Commons and the help which can be given to the provinces must be given under that crop insurance plan.
That is the story for the provinces of Quebec and Ontario.
I would now like, Mr. Chairman, to compare how the same Minister of Agriculture and his predecessor dealt with a problem absolutely similar to this one and involving the apple growers and farmers of British Columbia. I would not like any one to think that my words are dictated by spite or envy against the fruit growers of British Columbia, but 1 would like the same policy to be applied everywhere.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member continues to refer to the province from which I come as Columbie-Britannique. Its correct name is British Columbia.

Well, Mr. Chairman, if that can restore the good mood of my colleague, I am ready to accept his correction. But that must not prevent the house from realizing that there is a tremendous difference between the way the matters have been settled as far as the farmers in the province of my hon. friend are concerned and the apple-growers in my area and in south-western Ontario.
If hon. members want to refer to Hansard of May 3, 1965, the first answer given to a question put by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh) was that there was a crop insurance program and that the assistance given by the federal government should be provided through the crop insurance plan, which would force the provinces
November 9, 1966

to participate in the crop insurance scheme voted in this house.
But there is a fact which we should keep in mind, Mr. Chairman; between the time the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary put his question and the time the matter was settled, a general election was called. At that time, the Liberal government, for political advantage, I think, granted a subsidy of $4 million to British Columbia for assistance to apple-growers.
I repeat it, I am happy that the farmers of another province have received assistance because anyone who knows about the damages suffered by fruit-growers when their trees are destroyed, knows that these damages are tremendous.
Fruit-trees take five to ten years before they yield as much as the ones which were destroyed. I was therefore happy when I learned that the farmers of British Columbia had received assistance from the federal government. But I think there is injustice and discrimination by the present Liberal government in the case of farmers of the province of Quebec and those of southwestern Ontario.
I ask Quebec members to convince the Minister of Agriculture that as long as he applies one policy for eastern Canada and one for western Canada, as long as he will treat the farmers differently because they come from different provinces, he will impair national unity.
I ask them to convince their colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, to discharge his responsibility with equal fairness to everybody. Nothing is more apt to create animosity among the various groups concerned than the way the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) has tried to settle those two different cases.

Now, Mr. Chairman, should this plan we have heard about materialize, it would cause additional expenditures to a lot of workers of

my riding whenever they have to go and get their unemployment insurance benefits.
I would therefore ask the Minister of Labour to take the interest of my constituents into account and not close down the St. Hyacinthe unemployment office.

On two different occasions, those labour leaders met all members of parliament, Liberals, Conservatives, Independents, Credi-tistes, to submit representations and request our co-operation to convince the responsible minister to revise Bill C-170 and also the powers of the C.C.R.O. Mr. Speaker, in reply to the question raised last Thursday by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot, I wish to inform him that I have received a letter from the Quebec Department of Agriculture, asking whether the federal government was prepared to contribute to assistance for apple growers, whose crops were damaged by a hail storm last June.
In my reply, I indicated to the minister that my predecessor and myself had made it clear to the provinces, last year, that, in the future, federal assistance contributions on account of crop losses would be granted through a crop insurance scheme.
Such was the minister's reply, and he made the same reply to the member for Okanagan-Boundary, and then granted $4 million to British Columbia farmers.

In all frankness, Mr. Chairman, I do not feel that this reply could be interpreted as being a refusal since, definitely, I feel-and he is a witness himself-that, under

the previous government, there have been policies favouring certain provinces, most of them naturally in western Canada, and that we, in eastern Canada, always had to resort to a sort of begging policy.
Other considerations must also be brought forward. I feel that, in order to be explicit and make the truth known clearly, it is partly true that one period was more difficult because of the strike by hail but there is also another very important factor in this analysis, and it is what I might call the "depolliniza-tion" or the periodic lack of pollen in flowers, one of the natural causes often very difficult to explain.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
All I know is that I agree, in principle, with the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot when he says that farmers must be helped as much and as quickly as possible, because agriculture is a source of plenty. In years to come, farm production will not satisfy the demand, if we cannot assure the farmer of an adequate income.
I am very pleased to see that this government greatly favoured farm assistance, especially through its dairy policy and also its crop insurance plan. But I agree with the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot no doubt and with his colleagues from Quebec that our farmers must no longer beg, because that is not interesting for anyone, it is even disarming in some circumstances. To avoid wasting time on petty matters of politics or haggling, what we need is a crop insurance legislation approved by Quebec and Ottawa, so that from now on our farmers will be able to survive and keep their operations going thanks to legislation which will guarantee their prosperity.

The hon. member for Shef-ford (Mr. Neveu) will not have to waste much time or breath to convince us that crop insurance legislation is needed. He w;ll recall that we were responsible for having the Crop Insurance Act passed. Therefore, since we had it passed, it means that we understood the needs of the farming community in that regard.
But the hon. member for Shefford can talk and try to play down the effects of the refusal of his Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene), but the fact remains that the federal Minister of Agriculture, a Liberal, refused to the apple growers of Quebec and the farmers in southwestern Ontario what he gave to another province.

Mr. Chairman, I was unfortunately unable to be in the house during the whole of yesterday evening when the Minister of National Defence made another of his reassuring speeches to the house. However, the few times that I was present I noticed that not too many hon. members were in attendance, and perhaps I can be forgiven for suggesting that not everybody reads every word he says. Therefore, perhaps the house should have the benefit of taking another close look at what the minister said. The minister having been so careful to point out how fair and scrupulous he is, I think I should do the same, and I am sure he will appreciate a careful look at the words and statements he uttered last night.
For instance, as found on page 9714 of Hansard he said:
I have no fear whatsoever of further questions, and I fully expect that when we reach the committee stage hundreds of questions will be asked. This is a perfectly logical thing to happen.
The minister says he has no fear of further questions, but the truth is that his actions show he fears them more than anything. Certainly anyone who has no fear of further questions would expect questions to be asked and answers to be given when those questions and answers will do members of this house some good by augmenting their knowledge of unification. I therefore suggest it will be most entertaining to place the truth next to the minister's statements. He suggests he is not afraid of the questions, but the truth, which is evidenced by his actions, is simply that this is what he fears most.
As found on page 9715 of Hansard he said in another part of his speech:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot give the specific dates on which various views were made known but I assume they are known now in advance of second reading and therefore are fully available to my hon. friend in making up his mind in respect of the principle involved in this bill.
The minister says that the views are fully available but the truth is, as evidenced by army orders and by the action of the minister reminding the witnesses of their orders, that any serving officer in the forces is duty bound to keep quiet no matter how much he is opposed. He cannot make his views known and he cannot express himself. The only time he would be allowed to express his opinions would be if he were summoned before the house and given the protection of the house to speak the truth honestly and without fear of consequences. The minister says that all

the views are fully available but the truth is he knows very well they are not available.

The hon. member is therefore fully capable of taking his responsibility as a member of this house and in the knowledge of all the factors involved making a responsible judgment.

I will send my hon. friend a list. There are many lessons to be learned. We, as individuals elected by the people of this country to do the best job we can, are perfectly capable, after having listened to all the arguments pro and con, of making up our own minds.

They have all complained about the present situation of the armed services.
Vice Admiral Rayner goes on to say:
This procedure reminded me of the blackout in wartime Britain. Apparently we were to feel our way from lamp post to lamp post down the dimly lit and foggy street of integration.
It is time that the minister presented to the house the true facts regarding the position of the forces in respect of unification. As I have said before, probably the day after tomorrow the minister will parade before a cenotaph somewhere in the country in honour of the war dead and in honour of the regiments, the naval units and the air squadrons of which they were members. In spite of this, the minister wants to wipe out the whole history of the armed forces. I refer him to the statements he made at the time of the amalgamation of the militia units. At that time he thought it was a terrible thing. I remind him of the dishonest approach of his government in deciding to cancel the Arrow aircraft. I am referring to these matters because they are pertinent.
In referring to the decision of his own government to cancel the Arrow, a decision which was delayed until after the election,
November 9, 1966

the minister expressed the opinion that this was the worst possible decision that could have been made in Canadian military history and that it would be regretted for years to come. The minister shakes his head. Does he want more proof? He denied he had broken the confidence of senior officers and yet I can quote his own words from Hansard. I repeat, the minister shakes his head, but whom is he trying to impress? The minister made a denial a few minutes ago. I used his own words and threw them back in his face. Again I ask the minister to get up and to count on the fingers of one hand the countries who would let their defence ministers get away with what he is trying to get away with without putting them behind bars. I refer to countries in what we look upon as the free world. I would go further and ask what might happen to the minister in some other countries I can think of.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Admiral Rayner continues:
I assume that we were not called-
Before the committee that is.
-because I had expressed my concern to members of the government-
Just repeat what you said yesterday. That will be quite in order.
We have heard enough of him.
I always take a rest when you are around, Joe. You never interfere in anything. You never get on your feet here.
Don't worry about that.

He is
the same member who failed to show up at a do in his own riding a couple of years ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I must advise the hon. member for Cape Breton South that his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, the hon. member just said that I was the member who had failed to appear at what I would call a Tory meeting. In the result the hon. member himself was there, and instead of his presence being a hindrance to me he improved my chances of being elected.

Mr. Chairman, on the question of privilege-and I am sure my hon. friend from the New
Interim Supply
Democratic Party also has a question of privilege here-this meeting was not a Tory meeting. There were two representatives from the Conservative party, two from the New Democratic Party but only one from the Liberals because the hon. member failed to show up to discuss a matter of vital importance to the welfare of his own constituents. The hon. member for Timmins could back that up.

Mr. Chairman, because I have been brought into this question of privilege I think I should put the record straight. I recall very clearly that that meeting was called by the Kapuskasing labour council, not by the Conservative party, the Liberal party or the New Democratic Party.
It was called on behalf of the N.D.P., or rather the former C.C.F.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Not quite that easily, Mr. Chairman. If any hon. member opposite wants to speak next I will relinquish the floor to him.
The minister has no support from his side of the house.

I realize that. The debate has taken on a new and added emphasis today, indeed, during the past week. We have seen the achievement of one of the objectives of the opposition in the reaction of the press from one coast to the other. The objective to which I refer as having been achieved, and achieved in spite of the opposition on the part of government members, has been the shedding of some light on the implications and ramifications of what it is that the minister intends to do and the speed of the course he is following in order to do it.
It is not my intention today, nor has it ever been in the past, to bring personalities into this question, though it is suggested by the minister that this is what we are doing. It is much too serious a matter for that sort of thing. Without going into the purely regional aspects of the impact and effect of total unification, let alone integration, on one of our more basic economic services in the mari-times. there is much that can be said and much that still needs to be said to further the goal of informing the public of Canada of our fears and hesitations about granting the minister's request for approval in principle of the

November 9, 1966
Interim Supply
bill prior to its being referred to a committee for full and exhaustive study.
I hope the minister does not during the course of the next few days-indeed I am sure he will not-lose sight of one or two basic considerations. One of the principal considerations in our own sovereignty, the ultimate question of whether we are to muster and sustain our own defence forces or whether simply by default we are to turn this responsibility over to our neighbour to the south.
In the minister's 1964 white paper on defence he sugested quite strongly that the defence of North America is, indeed, indivisible, that it must be a joint undertaking by both the United States of America and Canada. I ask the minister not to lose sight of the possibility that some of us on this side of the house may be right in thinking that we as a nation are big enough, on the eve of our 100th birthday, to undertake our own defence and to meet the obligations that we have in a free world to the residents of Canada. Surely we are not to wipe out the efforts of 250 years and at the stroke of a pen end these things upon which our nation has been built. They are much more basic and of greater importance than the mere stroke of a pen which would implement the whim and desire of one man.
The question is of such great importance that the people of Canada, who are directly affected by the policy of the government of the day, must accept and respect this policy should it become law. In return for that respect the government should have some concern for their view, for their well-being and for their opinions. This has not yet been apparent in view of the adamant position taken by the minister, but I am still hopeful that he will change his mind and will come to realize that, in the absence of a reassessment of integration and its impact upon the services at this time, it would not be in the best interests of the country to rush headlong into the next step in the program, unification.
In the white paper on defence of 1964 the government made this suggestion in the concluding paragraphs:
In this paper no attempt has been made to set down hard and fast rules for future policy and development. The paper is a charter, a guide, not a detailed and final blueprint. The policy outlined in it is not immutable. It can be altered or adapted to meet the requirements of changing circumstances, national and international.
[Mr. Forrestall.l
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Surely, Mr. Chairman, this is a new concept. This is a new understanding of defence. This is an attempt to bring about drastic modifications of traditional defence concepts. Surely the spirit of this was broad enough to accommodate the real anguish, the real desires of the Canadian people. Surely the minister is broad enough to accept different points of view, to accept the possibility that he is not totally right, that somewhere along the line what may or may not be a good idea has run into snags, has run aground on reefs and needs reviewing. Surely what I have referred to suggests that, and not the rigid, immovable position put to us earlier today by the Prime Minister.
Surely the government can accommodate the possibility that there is another point of view, that possibly senior serving officers who have been discharged or released from the services may be right, and that possibly they are not hidebound by tradition. Possibly these men are concerned about national interests. Possibly they are true Canadians. Surely the government can accept this possibility. We do not yet live in a police state. Surely people who have points of view can be afforded a forum to express them and have them taken into consideration. Is that not the exercise of government?
I suggest that it is just possible for the government to be wrong. We may never be able to undo what we are being asked to do blindly. On this question mark the opposition parties and the government and its supporters on the other side of the house would leave themselves open to the charge of having failed to uphold the best interests of the nation if they permit the minister to pursue his course of action before there is a reasoned and rational review of this matter by members of the house and particularly by members of the defence committee.
All that we are asking, all that the emotion of the last week or so boils down to, is that the minister adopt a more reasonable attitude and let us pause now in the course of integration in order to reassess it. Let us see if the supporting civilian integrated services are compatible with the objectives of our national defence policy. Let us assess if the integrated command is able to fulfil our existing international obligations and the enduring obligations of the government to the people of the country.
I do not like to go into details or to inject parochial matters into debate, but the minister has suggested that Canada has the most
November 9, 1966

meaningful underwater detection force in the world. This is an interesting observation. It is true when one thinks of our ability to detect and track underwater movement. But the minister stops there. If the facts are alluded to by people questioning the minister he says, "I know better". Mr. Chairman, I know better. I know that ships are tied to the dock. I know it is not our role to keep them constantly at sea chasing submarines, real or imagined. What does concern me is our ability to put a ship to sea once a message is received through our tracking system that action is required. I make this point to emphasize the need to catch our second breath and take a look at the meaningful things in our defence posture.
I wish to refer to partially classified information and for that reason I ask this question in a rhetorical sense only. If the assumption behind the question is wrong I wish to be corrected. Let me put it this way. I should like to be satisfied that in the event of an emergency we can meet our commitments in the waters off our coasts, both east and west. I am not certain that we can meet them. Indeed, with the continuing falling of R.C.N. strength, the continuing rumours of lay-offs in our military establishments in Halifax, I doubt that we can meet our commitments. In spite of the gracious assurance of the Associate Minister of National Defence the other day, 30 people received notices today that they would be laid off on November 15, and 32 firemen at H.M.C.S. Shearwater were advised they were being transferred elsewhere as their role was being taken over by others. These things scare me.
Until we pause and reflect on integration and its impact on our efficiency and defence capability, we not only are not able to pursue with reason and understanding the measure to come before us but we shall be doing a great disservice to the people of this country by pursuing it. That the minister is in a difficult position is understandable, because steps toward the implementation of unification have been going on for a long time. The passage of the bill will make legal that which has already been done.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Before me I have a message. It may be classified, though it has appeared on bulletin boards in the dockyard, at H.M.C.S. Stadacona and possibly, one would hope, at military bases throughout Canada. Though the establishment where it appeared is an integrated, unified, or whatever name the minister calls
Interim Supply
it establishment, it is still a naval establishment. The document is dated Tuesday, November 1, 1966, and reads:
For the information of all concerned it is advised that an officers' integrated seniority policy has been adopted as follows:
Note the use of the past tense.
(a) Promotion to major and to higher ranks normally will be effected as vacancies occur.
And so on. Has the minister no feelings about these men who are to be transferred from the navy to something else? Mr. Bob Chambers, our beloved Nova Scotia cartoonist, has for a long time called it the "Nair-my", and perhaps he is right.
It is not our intention to let principles go by undealt with and unrecognized. These things must be brought to the attention of the Canadian public. This is the first and most useful opportunity we have had of doing so. The Canadian people must be told the extent to which the minister has gone in the field of unification and integration because ultimately the decision is theirs.
At regular intervals in military establishments in my area the authorities keep posting notices with regard to the disclosure of military information or opinions. I should like the minister to reassure those in the armed services that if they wish, and if they believe it necessary, they are free to speak to their members of parliament. My mail on the subject has been extremely heavy. If it were not for the consequences to the men and women who have expressed their fears about the results of integration and unification I would bring these letters into the house, dump them on the minister's desk and ask him to read them. There are nearly 3,000 of them.
It is interesting to note the sequence of events. Every time things get a little hot in the services and another blind step is taken toward furthering integration or unification I get a flurry of letters from young men and women who are deeply concerned about their future in the armed services. Shortly afterwards there invariably follows a notice calling the attention of members of the services to sections in the Queen's regulations prohibiting members of the armed forces from talking to people such as myself, I suppose. I will read one such notice into the record:
QR & O 19.36, 19.37 and 19.375 pertain to communications or disclosure of military information or opinions to individuals or news media. QR & O 19,375 provides that officers commanding commands, base commanders and COS may make suitable communications to news media on matters of interest

November 9, 1966
Interim Supply
concerning their commands provided no expressed or implied enunciation, defence or criticism of service, departmental or government policy is involved. Other officers and men are required to seek permission prior to disclosing military information or expressing their views on military matters.
Incidentally, I have a note from a young service officer in relation to the instruction I read earlier regarding promotion. He asks whether this is permitted at a time when parliament has not yet consented to the passage of some sort of unification bill, something, he adds, which he hopes will happen. He is referring to the command rank structure arrangements which are announced before even acceptance in principle has been given by this house.
The men in the services are deeply concerned. The hundreds and hundreds of letters which I receive on the subject all express real, not imaginary, concern, even though some of their fears may be based on a lack of full understanding. These men, in the particular instances to which I have referred, must ply their skills and trades at sea. No other form of work in this world, let alone in the armed forces of Canada, demands the skills, the temperament, the dedication which is demanded of men who follow the sea for their livelihood.
All we ask is a chance to pause, to stop this headlong rush. The minister said many times in the early stages of this program that this was a ten-year plan. Well, it was brought in two years ago and already we are into the final stage. What has happened to the ten-year plan? Where is it now? Has it been abandoned? Flexibility was another point. I am quoting now from a document called "Highlights Of The White Paper". I do not know where it came from. It speaks of flexibility to meet a wide range of possible uses. Yes, we shall all hear a lot at a later date about the real "sleeper" in the unification bill, the section dealing with the special force.
Does this refer to what the chief of the defence staff has said, I understand, on four occasions in Vancouver, Ottawa, Toronto and again in Toronto, namely, that the role of the Royal Canadian Navy is to be reduced to that of fleet transfer? "Sealift" is the word which is being used.
The minister sits there looking arrogant. He talks about pursuing his program. When will he call tenders for his four new ships?
How does one look arrogant? What is the impression one has to give? I don't know.
The minister does not need to practice. It comes out all over him.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Six o'clock.
Progress reported.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say to the acting house leader that I presume that tomorrow the unification bill will be referred to the defence committee without receiving second reading in the house and we will be able to get on with other business. I am wondering what that other business will be.

Mr. Speaker, so that there will be no misunderstanding I had better put the business clearly on the record. It is proposed to call interim supply again tomorrow, to be followed by item 101, second reading of Bill C-241, to amend the National Housing Act, and then it is proposed to call item 82, house in committee of the whole on Bill C-227, the medicare bill.
It being three minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, November 10, 1966
